title: Russia's Road to El Dorado
gist: Five years into Russia's Mali deployment, neither Wagner nor its successor Africa Corps has ever secured the gold-mining access that made the Central African Republic profitable, and the author argues Russia is now staying in Mali mainly out of sunk-cost inertia while its diplomatic and military position visibly erodes to jihadist attacks and rising Turkish drone influence.

themes.theme: Russia's failed resources-for-security model in Mali

insights.claim: Unlike in the Central African Republic, where Wagner became the guarantor of national security in exchange for full access to the state bureaucracy and economic access from gold and diamond mining to beer and liquor sales, Wagner failed to secure Mali's gold mining industry, and its successor Africa Corps has likewise failed to gain the access despite continuing the deployment for five years.
insights.speaker: Raphael Parens
insights.so_what: Establishes that Russia's Africa security-for-resources playbook, which worked in CAR, has structurally failed in Mali — a key differentiator for assessing which African states are actually vulnerable to Russian resource capture versus merely hosting Russian troops.
insights.quote: Wagner’s failure to secure extractive resources in Mali was the beginning of the end for the organization, but Africa Corps — an organization directly beholden to the Russian state — has also failed to secure access to Malian gold after taking Wagner’s place.
insights.locator: When the Wagner Group, Africa Corps’ predecessor, entered Mali...

insights.claim: Mali's 2023 mining code increased government royalties and ownership stakes in mines, and after arresting four Barrick Gold employees and issuing an arrest warrant for CEO Mark Bristow in late 2024, Mali forced Barrick into a roughly $430 million settlement to free employees, drop charges, and resume operations; President Assimi Goïta then centralized state gold mining ownership through the new venture Sopamim.
insights.speaker: Raphael Parens
insights.so_what: Documents a specific, large ($430M) state-coercion precedent against a major Western gold miner (Barrick) that both strengthened the Malian state's control over mining and squeezed out Russian access — a template risk for other foreign miners operating under juntas, and evidence Mali is centralizing resource nationalism rather than ceding it to Moscow.
insights.quote: Barrick and the Malian government then agreed to a settlement where Barrick would pay the state approximately $430 million in exchange for the freeing of its employees, dropped charges, and the renewal of operations.
insights.locator: Wagner was unable to gain a foothold in Mali's gold mining industry itself...

insights.claim: U.S. intelligence sources cited in the article claim Mali's junta government paid Wagner roughly $10.8 million per month, financed predominantly through taxes on international gold-mining firms like Barrick or direct gold contributions when payments dried up, keeping actual economic power in the hands of Bamako rather than Moscow.
insights.speaker: Raphael Parens
insights.so_what: A specific (though unverifiable, per the author) monthly payment figure ($10.8M) quantifying the actual cash flow to Wagner — useful as a rough scale reference, but the author explicitly flags it as guesswork without a clear paper trail.
insights.quote: Wagner was being paid by the Malian junta government roughly $10.8 million per month.
insights.locator: While Wagner could not secure gold mining access themselves...

insights.claim: RUSI's assessment, cited by the author, concludes that even if Wagner's Mali profits accrued fully to the Russian state rather than to Yevgeny Prigozhin personally, they would likely not be enough to cover the cost of a single day of Russia's fighting in Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Raphael Parens
insights.so_what: A striking scale comparison showing Mali's economic value to Russia is trivial relative to Ukraine war costs, reinforcing the thesis that continued Russian presence in Mali is not financially rational and is better explained by inertia/political capital than profit.
insights.quote: even if the yearly profits accrued to the Russian state and not to [former Wagner leader Yevgeny] Prigozhin (which seems very unlikely), in all likelihood they would not be enough to pay the costs of only one day of Russia’s fighting in Ukraine.
insights.locator: Regardless, the Royal United Services Institute for Defence and Security Studies argues...

insights.claim: Russian conglomerate Yadran Group broke ground on a gold processing facility in Mali in June 2025, but it will need to compete with the Malian-owned Marena Gold refinery and informal smelters in Bamako's central market, and its completion timeline is unclear amid a West African track record of failed or stalled foreign business projects.
insights.speaker: Raphael Parens
insights.so_what: A named, trackable Russian commercial project (Yadran gold facility) whose completion or failure would be a concrete signal of whether Russia can finally monetize its Mali presence.
insights.quote: this facility would need to compete with a Malian-owned refinery, Marena Gold, and makeshift smelters in Bamako’s central market
insights.locator: Africa Corps and the Kremlin have attempted to keep the pressure on Bamako.

insights.claim: Wagner suffered an estimated 84 troops killed in an ambush at Tinzaouatène in late July 2024, and Africa Corps continues to lose helicopters, face troop attacks and besieged bases, while being unable to stop jihadist attacks across Mali including in Bamako and along national highways — the author states Russian operations have not succeeded where Western forces failed.
insights.speaker: Raphael Parens
insights.so_what: Documents concrete, ongoing Russian military losses and operational failure in Mali (84 dead at Tinzaouatène, helicopter losses, unchecked jihadist attacks) — evidence that Russia's Sahel counterterrorism value proposition is not being delivered, undermining its remaining diplomatic capital there.
insights.quote: Wagner saw an estimated 84 troops killed during an ambush at Tinzaouatène in late July 2024, and Africa Corps continues to see its helicopters shot down, its troops attacked, and its bases besieged.
insights.locator: Instead, these fading diplomatic victories are proving to be a costly ongoing military venture.

insights.claim: The arrival of three new medium-range Turkish Akinci drones in Mali could signal a shift toward Turkish military assistance, following the drone-first strategy already adopted by fellow Alliance of Sahel States member Burkina Faso — a shift the author says would itself signal a weakened Malian state unable to sustain ground forces nationwide.
insights.speaker: Raphael Parens
insights.so_what: Identifies Turkey (via Akinci drone sales) as the rising alternative security partner displacing Russian influence in the Sahel — a concrete geopolitical rotation to track for Turkish defense-export growth and Russian influence decline in West Africa.
insights.quote: The arrival of three new medium-range Akinci drones could signal a shift toward Turkish military assistance, following the strategy of fellow Alliance of Sahel States partner Burkina Faso.
insights.locator: The Kremlin also faces challengers in its diplomatic campaign in Bamako.

insights.claim: A 2025 campaign by Al-Qaida affiliate Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin established a fuel blockade on Mali's capital and key cities, one of the country's most damaging defeats in the past two years, occurring alongside the death of pro-Russian junta Defense Minister Sadio Camara.
insights.speaker: Raphael Parens
insights.so_what: A concrete jihadist military success (nationwide fuel blockade) demonstrating the practical failure of the Russian-backed counterterrorism mission — relevant for assessing Mali's political stability and the risk of a further pro-Russian regime realignment or collapse.
insights.quote: a particularly damaging 2025 campaign that saw Al-Qaida affiliate Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin establish a fuel blockade on the capital and key cities
insights.locator: Mali has seen significant defeats over the past two years...

insights.claim: China's military investment in Mali has been limited to weapons and equipment sales (e.g., Norinco VP11 MRAP vehicles later captured by Tuareg forces at Tinzaouatène), constrained by Mali's lack of port infrastructure that China typically seeks and by the country's current instability discouraging China's preferred long-term investment model.
insights.speaker: Raphael Parens
insights.so_what: Explains why China remains a marginal player in Mali despite deeper involvement elsewhere in Africa — a useful comparator for gauging where China will versus won't expand influence based on infrastructure and stability prerequisites.
insights.quote: Mali lacks the port infrastructure that China has preferred to pursue in Africa, and the current level of instability in the country does not favor China’s brand of long-term investment.
insights.locator: China and the United Arab Emirates are smaller players in Mali...

insights.claim: UAE investment in Mali has centered on a $50 million payoff to Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin for the release of a kidnapped Emirati prince and another citizen — a payment a UN report linked to funding that group's broader offensive and the wider Al-Qaida network — and future Emirati investment in the Malian government will hinge on the conclusion of Sudan's civil war, where the UAE backs the Rapid Support Forces.
insights.speaker: Raphael Parens
insights.so_what: Reveals an indirect UAE linkage (ransom payment) to the same jihadist network destabilizing Mali, and ties future UAE-Mali engagement to the unrelated Sudan conflict outcome — a non-obvious cross-regional connection relevant for Gulf-Africa geopolitical risk mapping.
insights.quote: U.A.E. investment in Mali has centered around a $50 million payoff to Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin for a kidnapped Emirati prince and another citizen, which a United Nations report recently linked to that group’s offensive and payments to the broader Al-Qaida Network.
insights.locator: China and the United Arab Emirates are smaller players in Mali...

themes.theme: Why Russia stays: sunk cost, not strategy

insights.claim: The author's central thesis is that Russia is likely staying in Mali due to inertia and sunk-cost reasoning rather than any compelling strategic or economic rationale, since Mali's landlocked position in the Sahel has been a logistical burden (requiring air bridges from Syria and Libya and port agreements in Togo) rather than a strategic asset for other operations.
insights.speaker: Raphael Parens
insights.so_what: A contrarian read against the assumption that Russia's Sahel presence is a calculated strategic win — implies Russia's Mali position is more fragile and reversible than commonly assumed, raising the probability of a sudden Russian drawdown if triggered by another military setback.
insights.quote: At this point, Russia may be staying put in Mali due to inertia and sunk cost theory... Its location has been a bane rather than a boon for Russia.
insights.locator: At this point, Russia may be staying put in Mali due to inertia...

insights.claim: The author advises that another major attack on Bamako (particularly on the airport or government buildings), or another defeat on the scale of Tinzaouatène, could force Goïta's hand against Russia or prompt Africa Corps to evacuate on its own terms — creating a potential opening for the West, though any U.S./Western re-engagement should avoid the same security-for-resources trap that ensnared Russia and would require offering the lethality against civilians that Mali's junta wants but that the U.S. and France previously refused.
insights.speaker: Raphael Parens
insights.so_what: Identifies specific trigger events (attack on Bamako airport/government buildings, another Tinzaouatène-scale defeat) that would signal an imminent Russian exit from Mali — actionable watch-points for Sahel geopolitical risk monitoring.
insights.quote: Another major attack on Bamako, particularly on the airport or governmental buildings, could force Goïta’s hand against Russia. Likewise, another jarring defeat like Tinzaouaténe could see the Africa Corps evacuate on its own terms.
insights.locator: Policymakers in Washington and Paris should recognize the Russian weakness in Mali...
